p: In seventeen eighty-four, a Prussian newspaper asked its readers the question, what is enlightenment? The most famous answer came from the philosopher Immanuel Kant of Königsberg, a man of such regular habits that, it is said, the people of the town set their watches by his afternoon walk. Enlightenment, he wrote, is man's emergence from his self-imposed immaturity, which is the inability to use one's own understanding without the guidance of another. Its motto, he said, should be a phrase from the Roman poet Horace, sapere aude, which means dare to know, or have the courage to use your own understanding. That is as good a definition as any of the movement of thought that dominated Europe in the eighteenth century, and of which my own age is the heir, and, in some respects, the critic.

The Enlightenment had no single leader and no single doctrine. It was a temper rather than a creed: a confidence that the methods which Newton had applied to the heavens could be applied to human affairs, to government, law, religion, economics and education, and that by the use of reason mankind could free itself from superstition, tyranny and cruelty and make itself happier. Its centre was France, where its writers were called the philosophes, the French word for philosophers, but it flourished also in Scotland, England, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and America.

Its English roots lay in John Locke, who argued in his Essay Concerning Human Understanding that the mind at birth is a blank slate, written upon by experience, so that men are made by their education and circumstances; and in his Two Treatises of Government that men have natural rights to life, liberty and property, that governments exist to protect those rights, and that a government which violates them may be resisted. In France, Voltaire, the wittiest man in Europe, spent a long life mocking the intolerance of the Church, whose cruelties he summed up in the phrase écrasez l'infâme, meaning crush the infamous thing, and campaigning to clear the name of Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant of Toulouse who had been tortured and executed on a false charge of murdering his son to prevent his conversion. Montesquieu, in The Spirit of the Laws, argued that liberty is best preserved when the powers of government, to make laws, to execute them and to judge, are separated and balance one another; the founders of the United States read him carefully. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, a strange, unhappy and enormously influential Swiss, argued that man is good by nature and corrupted by society, and that the only legitimate government rests on the general will of the people.

Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert edited the great Encyclopédie, a French word meaning encyclopaedia, in seventeen volumes of text and eleven of plates, between seventeen fifty-one and seventeen seventy-two, intending, in Diderot's words, to change the common way of thinking. It described the trades and crafts of France with the same respect as theology and philosophy, and its articles slipped in criticism of Church and state under innocent headings. It was banned repeatedly and published anyway. I confess a professional affection for it, since I spend my nights reading its distant descendant.

In Scotland, David Hume, the most penetrating philosopher of the age, questioned whether we can know that causes produce effects, and whether miracles can ever be believed; and his friend Adam Smith, in The Wealth of Nations, argued that the wealth of a nation comes from the labour of its people and the division of that labour, and that men pursuing their own interest in a free market are led, as by an invisible hand, to serve the general good. Cesare Beccaria of Milan, in a short book On Crimes and Punishments, argued against torture and the death penalty, and was read by every reforming monarch in Europe.

Some of those monarchs, called the enlightened despots, tried to put these ideas into practice from their thrones: Frederick the Great of Prussia, who corresponded with Voltaire and abolished torture; Catherine the Great of Russia, who corresponded with Diderot and bought his library; and the emperor Joseph the Second of Austria, who granted toleration to Protestants and Jews and abolished serfdom, and found that his subjects resisted almost every one of his reforms. Enlightened despotism, it appeared, was more easily described than practised. A reforming tyrant is still a tyrant, and his reforms die with him.

The Encyclopaedia of the future is rightly severe on the Enlightenment's failures of consistency. Many of its champions of liberty owned slaves, or invested in the slave trade, or wrote that the peoples of Africa were naturally inferior. Most of them took for granted that women should be excluded from public life, though a few, such as the Marquis de Condorcet and the English writer Mary Wollstonecraft, whose Vindication of the Rights of Woman appeared in seventeen ninety-two, argued otherwise. And the faith in reason could become a faith of its own, as dogmatic as the religion it attacked.

Yet the Enlightenment's achievements are all about us. Religious toleration, freedom of the press, the abolition of torture, the idea of natural and universal human rights, the separation of powers, the rule of law, public education, and the conviction that the purpose of government is the happiness of the governed, all were the programme of the Enlightenment before they were the practice of any state. Its ideas were put to the test in two great revolutions, in America and in France, to which I shall now turn. One of them succeeded better than the other. The Enlightenment had taught that men could remake the world by reason. The French Revolution was to show how much blood that remaking might cost.
